title: Automation of a Train‐Carrying Prototype Rail Detection System Using a Camera Sensor Technology
content:
This study presents an automated camera-based railway track detection system for a train-carrying prototype, integrating image processing and optical flow on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX. Experimental results demonstrate 91.16% average detection accuracy and near-real-time performance of approximately 15 FPS at lorry speeds of 15–25 km/h.


ABSTRACT

This study discusses rail transport on the track provided by the rail, which has been a safety challenge. Accidents often occur when the lorry moves the train on the track, especially on bends in the rail, which causes the lorry to move incorrectly following the rail track even though it is controlled by the operator. With this research, based on the Z-cam E2-M4 camera running using NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX, which is a high-performance module for processing, this device will automatically identify the rail through image processing with the optical flow method, which is believed to be able to overcome track errors in real-time. This image-based technique is not just a simple technique but can function to recognize the railway mapping track by combining edge detection that transforms to isolate certain tracks based on the image sequence, thus keeping the lorry on track. From experiments conducted with a prototype scale on the installation of the train, the results showed an average success rate of 91.16% during the initial testing phase. A total of 10 tests were conducted using the same experimental parameters to evaluate the consistency of the proposed system. For clarity, the results of these 10 tests are represented in Section 4 by three representative track scenarios: straight track under low illumination, curved track, and straight track under high illumination, corresponding to different observation time windows of 00:07, 00:35, and 00:15, respectively. Across the subsequent evaluation of the 10 tests, the peak performance reached 96.7%. These figures are promising for a prototype at scale, although further field testing is needed to ensure the unit's survivability in real-world conditions, even in unpredictable weather conditions like those in Indonesia. This practical implementation is a first step toward addressing accident-related issues using optical flow methods, which are particularly useful in these situations.
